question: What phrases are repeated on each day of creation, and what changes on the sixth day compared with the others?
The verb בָּרָא (bara, “create”) appears in only three verses of the chapter: at what moments does the text use it, and what does that highlight?
What might it mean that human beings were created “in the image of God,” and how does this connect to the task of ruling over and caring for the earth?
God sees that everything “was very good”: how does this view of the created world affect the way you treat people and nature?
What is the man formed from, where is he placed, and what trees are in the middle of the garden?
Why does the chapter give the seventh day its own blessing and sanctification, if God creates nothing on it?
The verb יָצַר (yatsar, “form”) is the word for a potter shaping clay: what picture of God and of human beings does it suggest in verses 7 and 19?
God says “it is not good for the man to be alone”: what company and what help do you need today, and to whom could you be a helper?
How does the serpent alter God's words, and what steps does the woman take between seeing the tree and eating its fruit?
The word עֵירֹם (erom, “naked”) appears right after their eyes are opened: how does nakedness, which once caused no shame (2:25), become a reason for fear?
Which relationships are broken in the words spoken to the serpent, the woman and the man, and what does verse 15 leave open?
Faced with the question “Where are you?”, the man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent: how do you usually react when confronted with a mistake?
What offering do Cain and Abel bring, and how does the text describe Cain's reaction?
The word חַטָּאָה (chattaah, “sin”) appears for the first time in the Bible in verse 7, as something “at the door”: what image does the text use, and what should Cain do about it?
What contrast is there between the protection God gives Cain (v. 15) and Lamech's song of revenge?
“Am I my brother's keeper?”: for whom do you feel responsible, and where are you tempted to answer like Cain?
What formula is repeated in the life of each patriarch, and at what points do the stories of Enoch and Lamech depart from it?
The verb הָלַךְ (halak, “walk”) describes Enoch in verses 22 and 24: what does the expression “walk with God” suggest about his life?
Why does the chapter recall creation “in the likeness of God” and then say that Adam fathered Seth “in his own likeness”?
The phrase “and he died” is repeated almost to the end: how does remembering that life is limited change the way you use your time?
How does the text describe what the LORD sees in humanity, and what He feels about it?
The word חָמָס (chamas, “violence”) sums up the state of the earth in verses 11 and 13: what link does the text draw between human violence and the corruption of the whole earth?
What sets Noah apart from his generation, according to verses 8, 9 and 22?
Noah did “everything just as God had commanded him,” before he could see the flood: where do you need to obey before you understand the outcome?
What details of date and of the source of the waters does the text record about the start of the flood?
Why does the text make a point of saying that it was the LORD who shut the door of the ark?
The verb גָּבַר (gavar, “prevail, be strong”) is repeated for the waters: what does this repetition convey about the force of the flood?
“Only Noah was left”: how do you experience being in the minority when you choose to be faithful?
Which birds does Noah send out, how many times, and what does each return or absence teach him?
The chapter begins with the verb זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”): what does it mean in the Bible for God to “remember” someone, and what turning point does it mark in the story?
What changes in God's relationship with the earth after the flood, if the human heart is still “evil from his youth”?
The first thing Noah does when he leaves the ark is build an altar: how do you usually mark the new beginnings of your life?
What are the parts of the covenant described here: who establishes it, with whom, and what is the sign?
Why do blood and human life receive so much protection, and what reason does verse 6 give for it?
The word בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”) appears several times in this passage: how is this first covenant with all creation different from those that will follow?
Shem and Japheth cover their father without looking; Ham sees and tells: how do you act when you discover the weakness of someone close to you?
Which peoples descend from Japheth, Ham and Shem, and what elements does the text use to group them (vv. 5, 20, 31)?
What role does Nimrod have in the list, and why does the text mention Babel among the cities of his kingdom?
The word גּוֹי (goy, “nation”) closes the list in verse 32: what does it mean for the Bible to begin Israel's story with a view of all the nations?
The chapter shows a diverse humanity coming from a single family: how does this affect the way you see people of other peoples and languages?
What materials do the builders use, and what reasons do they themselves give for building the city and the tower?
The verb בָּלַל (balal, “confuse”) sounds like the name Babel: what wordplay does the text make in verse 9, and what does it say about the city's project?
The builders feared being “scattered,” and that is what happens: what does the text suggest about the desire to “make a name” for oneself?
The chapter ends with a family stopped at Haran and a barren woman: in what situation of your life does the story seem to have stopped halfway?
What does the LORD ask Abram to leave behind, and how many promises does He make next?
The word בְּרָכָה (berakhah, “blessing”) appears in verse 2, linked to “you will be”: what does it mean to be not only blessed but a blessing to others?
How does the episode in Egypt contrast with the faith shown at the start of the chapter, and who ends up suffering for Abram's lie?
Abram sets out without knowing the destination: what step do you feel you need to take without having the whole map?
Why does the quarrel between the herdsmen arise, and what proposal does Abram make to Lot?
What does Lot see when he chooses the plain of the Jordan, and what does verse 13 add that he does not seem to consider?
The verb פָּרַד (parad, “part, separate”) marks the decision of the chapter: what does the LORD say to Abram right after Lot “had parted from him”?
Abram gives up choosing first in order to keep the peace: in what conflict could you act this way?
How does Abram learn of Lot's capture, and with how many men does he set out to rescue him?
The title עֶלְיוֹן (elyon, “Most High”) is on the lips of Melchizedek and then of Abram: how does Abram take up this name in verse 22?
Who is Melchizedek according to the text, and why does Abram give him a tenth?
Abram refuses to profit from the wealth of the king of Sodom: what gains should you refuse in order to keep your integrity?
What complaint does Abram bring to the LORD, and how does the LORD answer using the stars?
The verb אָמַן (aman, “believe, trust”), the source of “amen,” appears in verse 6: what does the text say was “credited” to Abram, and why?
What might the ritual of the animals cut in two and the torch of fire passing between them mean, given that only the LORD passes through?
God says “Do not be afraid” before Abram voices his doubt: what fear would you bring to God today with the same frankness?
Who takes the initiative to give Hagar to Abram, and how does the relationship between Sarai and Hagar change after the pregnancy?
Hagar calls the LORD the God רֳאִי (roi, “who sees”): what does it mean for a runaway servant to name God from the experience of being seen?
Why does the angel tell Hagar to go back, and what promises does he make to her that recall those made to Abram?
“Where have you come from, and where are you going?”: how would you answer these two questions about your own life today?
What name does God use to introduce Himself, and what changes of name and promises does He announce to Abram?
The verb מוּל (mul, “circumcise”) is repeated many times: why is the sign of the covenant placed in the flesh itself, and who must receive it?
How do Abraham's laughter and his request for Ishmael reveal what he feels about the promise, and how does God answer each one?
“Walk before Me and be blameless”: what would it look like in your routine to live “before God”?
What gestures of hospitality does Abraham offer the three visitors, and with what haste does he act?
The verb צָחַק (tsachaq, “laugh”) appears three times in Sarah's scene: how is this laughter related to the name Isaac, promised in the previous chapter?
What does Abraham's bargaining over Sodom reveal about how he understands the justice of “the Judge of all the earth”?
Abraham intercedes for a city that is not his own: for whom could you speak before God with the same persistence?
How does Lot receive the visitors, and what do the men of Sodom demand of him?
Why does Lot hesitate to leave, and what does verse 16 say about the reason he was saved?
The verb נָבַט (nabat, “look”) appears in the angels' command and in the gesture of Lot's wife: what might that look back have meant?
The chapter ends with Lot isolated in a cave and decisions made out of fear: what choices of yours has fear already steered?
What does Abraham say about Sarah in Gerar, and how does God intervene with Abimelech?
What justification does Abraham give for repeating the half-truth of chapter 12, and what does it reveal about his fear?
The word תֹּם (tom, “integrity, innocence”) is used by Abimelech and confirmed by God: what does the text suggest about a foreigner acting with more integrity than Abraham?
Abraham, who did wrong, is still called to pray for Abimelech: what does this teach about serving others even after failing?
What words of Sarah at Isaac's birth take up the laughter of chapters 17 and 18, and how has the meaning of that laughter changed?
The verb פָּקַד (paqad, “visit, attend to”) opens the chapter: what does it mean that the LORD “visited” Sarah, and how does verse 1 stress the fulfillment of His word?
What parallels are there between this scene of Hagar in the wilderness and the one in chapter 16, and what does God do for her and the boy this time?
God “opened her eyes” and Hagar saw a well that was already there: when have you needed God to open your eyes to a way out?
How does God describe Isaac when He makes the request to Abraham, and what words of verse 2 make the request even heavier?
The verb נָסָה (nasah, “test”) appears right in verse 1: how does this information, given to the reader and not to Abraham, change the reading of the chapter?
How do you understand Abraham's answer to Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb,” and how have Jewish and Christian readings read this scene?
Abraham answers three times “Here I am”: to whom and in what situations have you said that phrase?
How does the negotiation between Abraham and the Hittites unfold, and why does Abraham insist on paying the price?
Abraham presents himself as a גֵּר (ger, “foreigner, sojourner”): what does it mean that the first land he owns in Canaan is a grave?
Why does the text describe the property, the trees and the witnesses of the purchase in such detail?
Abraham stops to weep for Sarah before solving the practical problems: what room do you give to grief in your life?
What sign does the servant ask of God, and how does Rebekah go beyond what he asked?
The word חֶסֶד (chesed, “loving devotion, loyalty”) appears in the servant's prayer and in the final request to Laban: what link does the chapter show between God's loyalty and human loyalty?
Why is it significant that the family asks Rebekah, and that she answers “I will go”?
The servant stops and worships as soon as he perceives God's guidance: how do you usually react when you recognize an answer to prayer?
What happens in Rebekah's pregnancy, and what answer does the LORD give her when she goes to inquire of Him?
What does “the older will serve the younger” mean, and where has this pattern already appeared in Genesis?
The word בְּכוֹרָה (bekhorah, “birthright”) is repeated in the exchange between Esau and Jacob: what was at stake in this right, and how does verse 34 judge Esau's attitude?
Esau trades something of great value for an immediate need: what pressures of the moment could lead you to give up what is important?
What command does the LORD give Isaac during the famine, and which promises made to Abraham does He repeat?
The verb רִיב (riv, “quarrel, dispute”) runs through the story of the wells: how does Isaac react to each quarrel, and what does the name Rehoboth express?
What similarities and differences are there between Isaac's lie about Rebekah and Abraham's in chapters 12 and 20?
Isaac would rather move on than keep fighting over wells: in what dispute of your life would it be better to move on?
What plan does Rebekah prepare, and what objection does Jacob raise before agreeing?
Isaac says Jacob came “deceitfully,” מִרְמָה (mirmah): how will this theme of deceit turn against Jacob later in his story?
Why can't Isaac simply undo the blessing given to Jacob, and what does the text suggest about the weight of a spoken word?
Esau's cry, “Bless me too,” shows the pain of someone who feels passed over: how do you deal with the feeling of having been left behind?
What does Jacob see in the dream, and what promises does the LORD make to him?
What does it mean for Jacob to discover that “the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it,” just as he is fleeing from home?
The stone that served as a pillow becomes a מַצֵּבָה (matsevah, “pillar”): why mark the place of an encounter with God with a visible sign?
Jacob's vow begins with “If God will be with me”: to what extent does your faith also have conditions, and how does God respond to that in the text?
How does Jacob's meeting with Rachel at the well take place, and how does Laban receive him?
Jacob asks Laban “Why have you deceived me?”, with the verb רָמָה (ramah, “deceive”): what irony is there in Jacob being deceived in place of the younger sister?
What do the names Leah gives her sons reveal about what she feels, and what changes with the name of Judah?
The LORD “saw that Leah was unloved”: what does it mean to you to know that God sees those who are left aside?
How does the rivalry between Rachel and Leah show up in the names they give their sons?
The verb קָנָא (qana, “be jealous, envy”) describes Rachel in verse 1: how does envy between sisters drive the whole first part of the chapter?
How does Jacob manage to prosper despite Laban's maneuvers, and to whom does he himself attribute this result?
Rachel says “Give me children, or I will die”: what have you made a condition for being happy, and how has it affected your relationships?
What reasons lead Jacob to decide to leave, and how do Rachel and Leah respond to his proposal?
The verb גָּנַב (ganav, “steal”) is repeated: what is “stolen” by Rachel, by Jacob and, according to Jacob, by those who held him accountable for lost animals?
How does Jacob sum up his twenty years of work for Laban, and to whom does he attribute leaving with possessions and not “empty-handed”?
Jacob and Laban end with an agreement and a heap of stones between them: what clear boundaries do you need to set in a difficult relationship?
What steps does Jacob take on learning that Esau is coming with four hundred men?
What does Jacob's prayer reveal about how he sees himself and God's promises?
The verb אָבַק (avaq, “wrestle”) sounds like Jabbok, the place of the struggle: what do this night struggle and the new name Israel say about Jacob's life?
“I will not let You go unless You bless me”: what have you been wrestling with before God, and what do you hope to receive?
In what order does Jacob arrange his family before Esau, and what does that order reveal?
The word חֵן (chen, “favor, grace”) appears three times on Jacob's lips: what does he hope to find in Esau's sight?
Why does Jacob say that seeing Esau's face was like seeing “the face of God,” right after Peniel?
Esau runs, embraces and weeps with the brother who deceived him: what reconciliation are you still hoping to live, or could you begin?
What does Shechem do to Dinah, and what proposal do he and Hamor present next?
The verb טָמֵא (tame, “defile”) appears in verses 5, 13 and 27: how does the text describe what happened to Dinah, and who speaks for her in the chapter?
How do you read the revenge of Simeon and Levi and Jacob's reaction, knowing that the text itself leaves the last question unanswered?
Jacob thinks of the danger to the household; the sons think of their sister's honor: how can we seek justice for those who were wronged without falling into violence?
What does Jacob ask of his family before going up to Bethel, and what do they hand over?
The expression “foreign gods” uses the word נֵכָר (nekhar, “foreign”): why does the return to Bethel require leaving these gods behind?
What elements of chapters 17 and 28 reappear in this new appearance of God to Jacob?
Rachel dies giving birth and calls her son Ben-oni; Jacob calls him Benjamin: how do you give a new name to a pain from your past?
Why does Esau separate from Jacob, and where does he go to live?
The word אַלּוּף (alluf, “chief of a clan”) is repeated in the list: what does Edom's organization into chiefs and kings show about the fulfillment of the blessing given to Esau?
Why does the text note that Edom had kings “before any king reigned over the Israelites”?
Genesis devotes a whole chapter to the descendants of Esau, the brother who did not inherit the promise: what might this say to you about the worth of those outside the main focus?
What factors feed the brothers' hatred of Joseph, according to verses 2 to 11?
Joseph's כְּתֹנֶת (ketonet, “robe, tunic”) appears at the beginning and the end of the chapter: how does this garment go from a sign of favor to false proof of death?
What different roles do Reuben and Judah take on in the face of the plot against Joseph, and what does each one intend?
Jacob “refused to be comforted”: how do you react when someone close to you is living a pain that seems to have no end?
What happens to Judah's first two sons, and what promise does he make to Tamar?
The verb נָכַר (nakar, “recognize”) appears here and in chapter 37 (vv. 32-33): what link does this repetition create between the deception of Jacob and what Judah now has to recognize?
What does it mean for Judah to say of Tamar “She is more righteous than I,” and what change does this begin to show in him?
Judah condemns Tamar quickly until he discovers his own guilt: in what situation do you judge others more harshly than yourself?
What expression is repeated to explain Joseph's prosperity in Potiphar's house?
The verb עָזַב (azav, “leave, abandon”) is repeated in the scene with Potiphar's wife: what does Joseph leave behind, and how is that garment used against him?
What reasons does Joseph give for refusing Potiphar's wife, and why does he speak of sinning “against God”?
Even in prison, the text says “the LORD was with Joseph”: how do you perceive God's presence in places you did not choose to be?
What dreams do the cupbearer and the baker have, and how does Joseph interpret each one?
What does Joseph mean by “Don't interpretations belong to God?”, and what attitude does this reveal in him?
The verb זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”) appears in Joseph's request and at the end of the chapter: what contrast does the text create between the request and the cupbearer's forgetfulness?
Joseph is forgotten by the one he helped: how do you deal with the ingratitude of those who received your kindness?
What are Pharaoh's two dreams, and why can't the magicians and wise men help him?
The word רוּחַ (ruach, “spirit”) describes Pharaoh's troubled spirit (v. 8) and the “Spirit of God” he recognizes in Joseph (v. 38): what contrast does the chapter draw between the two?
What do the names Manasseh and Ephraim say about the way Joseph understands his past and his present?
Joseph's plan is to store up in plenty for the time of scarcity: what does this practical wisdom suggest about the way you use your resources?
How does Joseph's first meeting with his brothers take place, and who recognizes whom?
The verb רָגַל (ragal, “spy”) appears in Joseph's repeated accusation: why does he insist on calling his brothers spies, and what does he want to find out?
What link do the brothers make between their present distress and what they did to Joseph, and why does Joseph weep as he listens to them?
“Surely we are being punished because of our brother”: what old guilt may still be weighing on your life, waiting to be acknowledged?
What arguments does Judah use to convince Jacob to let Benjamin go, and what steps does Jacob take?
The verb עָרַב (arav, “be surety, guarantee”) shows Judah offering himself as a pledge for Benjamin: what change is there between this Judah and the one who proposed selling Joseph in chapter 37?
What does Joseph feel when he sees Benjamin, and what might it mean to give him a portion five times larger?
Jacob says “If I am bereaved, I am bereaved”: how do you entrust to God what you most fear losing?
What trap does Joseph set with the silver cup, and how do the brothers react when it is found with Benjamin?
Why does Judah say that “God has exposed the iniquity of your servants,” if they did not steal the cup?
Judah takes up the verb עָרַב (arav, “be surety”) again in verse 32: how does his speech show that he now puts his brother's life and his father's pain above himself?
Judah offers to stay as a slave in his brother's place: for whom would you be willing to bear a personal cost?
How does Joseph reveal himself to his brothers, and what is their first reaction?
The word מִחְיָה (michyah, “preserving life”) sums up in verse 5 the way Joseph rereads his story: how does he combine his brothers' responsibility with God's action?
Joseph says “it was not you who sent me here, but God”: how does this reading coexist with the real evil the brothers did?
Joseph advises “Do not quarrel on the way”: what old accusations do you need to set aside after a reconciliation?
Where does Jacob stop before going down to Egypt, and what promises does God make to him in the visions of the night?
The verb יָרַד (yarad, “go down”) appears in God's words: what does it mean for God to say “I will go down with you to Egypt”?
Why does the text make a point of counting the people of Jacob's household who entered Egypt and reaching the number seventy?
Jacob says “Now I am ready to die, since I have seen your face”: what reunion or what answer have you been waiting for as long as he did?
What stages do the people of Egypt go through during the famine, and with what do they pay for bread each year?
Jacob calls his life מָגוּר (magur, “pilgrimage, sojourn”): what does this word reveal about how he understands his story before Pharaoh?
What does it mean for an old foreign shepherd to bless the most powerful king on earth, and to do it twice?
Jacob sums up his days as “few and hard”: how would you describe your story so far, and what would you like to change from here on?
How does Jacob place his hands when he blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, and how does Joseph react?
The word יָמִין (yamin, “right hand”) marks the hand of the main blessing: what pattern of Genesis repeats when Jacob places it on the younger?
How does Jacob describe God in the blessing, and what do the titles “the God who has been my shepherd” and “the Angel who has redeemed me” sum up about his life?
Jacob never expected to see Joseph's face, and God showed him even his grandchildren: in what area have you received more than you expected?
What does Jacob say to Reuben, to Simeon and Levi, and to Judah, and what explains the difference between these words?
In the middle of the blessings, Jacob exclaims “I await Your salvation, O LORD,” using יְשׁוּעָה (yeshuah, “salvation”): why does this prayer appear right there?
How have the words about Judah, with the scepter and the lion, been read in Jewish and Christian tradition, and what does the text itself leave open?
Each son receives his own word, according to his story: how do you receive hard or encouraging words about your character?
Why do the brothers fear Joseph after Jacob's death, and what message do they send?
The verb חָשַׁב (chashav, “intend, plan”) appears twice in verse 20: how does Joseph set the brothers' plan side by side with God's plan?
Why does Genesis end with Joseph asking them to carry up his bones, and what does this prepare for the next book?
Joseph refuses to take “the place of God” and chooses to provide for those who hurt him: how does this shed light on a forgiveness you need to give?
